opus-5.5.text:
That's a fun question. If I were in that seat, I think the first thing I'd remind myself is that Berkshire's edge has never been predicting technology. It's patience, discipline, and owning businesses with durable moats. So I wouldn't try to pretend to be a VC picking the winning model lab.

I'd probably think about it in three buckets.

The first, and maybe the biggest, would go to what I'd call the "picks and shovels" layer: energy, power infrastructure, data centers, cooling, grid. Whatever happens with models, compute needs electricity, and electricity needs physical assets that take years to build. That fits Berkshire's style really well. They already own utilities, and it's capital-intensive, long-horizon, and less sensitive to which lab wins. I'd put maybe 40% there.

The second bucket would be a few concentrated bets on frontier capability. I don't think you can ignore the possibility that a small number of players capture enormous value. But the lesson I'd take is: don't spread it thin across twenty labs. Pick the two or three you deeply understand, where you trust the people and the research culture, and be willing to hold through a lot of volatility. Maybe 25–30%.

The third bucket is what I personally find most interesting, which is the application and utility layer. Over the past couple of years I've come to believe we're moving into a "second half" of AI. In the first half, the game was about training methods and climbing benchmarks. Now the base capabilities are strong enough that the bottleneck is: what problems are actually worth solving, and how do you measure real utility in the real world? The value will come from companies that define new tasks, own the user relationship and context, and build products that get better with use. That's harder to spot, because it often doesn't look like an "AI company." It might look like a customer service business or a software company that quietly rebuilt itself around agents. So I'd keep the rest for that, and frankly, also as dry powder. Berkshire always keeps cash for when things get irrational, and AI will definitely have moments of irrationality in both directions.

And one more thing, which isn't really about allocation: I'd try to look at my own existing portfolio and ask which of those businesses get stronger with AI and which get disrupted. That might matter more than the fifty billion itself.

r001.rationale: The response makes no comparison to oil companies before cars.

r002.rationale: It says companies that own user relationships and context may create value, but does not clearly state that this ownership creates a strong competitive moat when AI intelligence is broadly accessible.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a fun framing, because Berkshire's whole philosophy is almost the opposite of how AGI money gets allocated today. Buffett wants businesses with durable moats, predictable cash flows, and management he can leave alone for twenty years. Almost nothing in AGI looks like that right now. So the first honest answer is that if I were really Berkshire's CEO, I might allocate a lot less than $50 billion, or at least I'd be very suspicious of my own excitement.

But if you force me to deploy it, I'd think about it in layers, roughly by how confident I am that the value is durable.

The first layer is the stuff that wins regardless of which lab wins. Compute, energy, and the physical supply chain. Whether the frontier ends up being OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, or some Chinese lab, they all need chips, data centers, power, and cooling. That's very Berkshire actually, it's like owning the railroad instead of betting on which shipper grows. I'd put a big chunk there, maybe 40 percent, and I'd lean toward the parts that are less obviously priced in, like power generation and grid infrastructure, rather than just buying Nvidia at whatever it costs today.

The second layer is the frontier labs themselves. This is where people get the most excited and where I'd be most careful. The problem is that the technology is improving fast, which sounds good, but fast improvement also means today's advantage erodes quickly. The gap between the top model and the third-best model keeps shrinking. So a lab's moat isn't really the model, it's distribution, data flywheels, and talent retention. I'd take maybe 20 percent and spread it across two or three labs rather than concentrate, because I genuinely don't think anyone can call the winner with confidence, including the people running the labs.

The third layer, and the one I'd personally be most interested in, is the application and agent layer. My own research has been about language agents, systems that don't just answer questions but act in environments, use tools, and complete long tasks. I think the next few years, a lot of the value capture moves from "who has the best model" to "who built the product where the agent actually does useful work reliably." Coding agents are the obvious first case because the environment is verifiable, you can run the tests. But I'd expect the same pattern in customer support, finance operations, scientific research tooling. The Berkshire-style question there is: which of these businesses have real switching costs and real workflow lock-in once the agent is embedded? That's harder to evaluate, so I'd put maybe 25 percent there, in a more venture-like structure, accepting that most will fail.

And then I'd keep the last 15 percent in cash. Not because I'm being cute, but because I think there's a reasonable probability of a correction in this space in the next few years, and the best Berkshire moves historically happened when everyone else needed liquidity. In 2008 they got to write the terms. Something like that will happen in AI too.

One more thing I'd say, which is less about the money and more about the mindset. Buffett's edge was always being able to say "I don't understand this, so I'll pass." In AGI, the honest version of that is that nobody fully understands the trajectory, including the researchers. So I'd want the allocation to be robust to being wrong about timelines in both directions. If AGI arrives in three years, the compute and energy bets pay off enormously. If it takes fifteen, the application businesses still generate real cash flow along the way. What I would avoid is any single bet that only works if one specific story is true.

r001.rationale: The response discusses infrastructure and AGI investment but does not compare companies holding user context to oil companies before cars were invented.

r002.rationale: The response identifies distribution, data flywheels, and workflow lock-in as possible moats, but does not argue that owning user context is a strong moat if AI intelligence becomes broadly accessible.

astra-6.text:
I’d first ask whether the goal is to generate returns or to accelerate AGI, because those are different investment problems. If I’m Berkshire’s CEO, I should care about returns. Even if I believe AGI will be transformative, that doesn’t mean every company building it is a good investment at any price.

I’d think about three layers: infrastructure, models, and applications. Infrastructure has relatively concrete demand, but you have to consider what happens if today’s spending doesn’t translate into sustainable revenue. Models could create enormous value, but competition might make it difficult for any one company to capture that value. Applications are interesting because you can ask a very practical question: does this system do useful work that someone will pay for?

So I wouldn’t immediately divide the entire $50 billion among those three categories. I’d invest gradually, looking for evidence of durable advantages. For an application company, that might be ownership of a customer relationship, integration into a workflow, or an ability to learn from real usage—not just access to a strong model that everyone else can also use.

And I’d look beyond companies labeled ‘AI.’ If intelligence becomes much cheaper, an existing business that can use it effectively might be a better investment than the company producing it. The key question is where the economic value stays as the technology improves. I’d want to understand that before committing all the money.

r001.rationale: The response makes no analogy to oil companies before cars; it discusses infrastructure, models, and applications instead.

r002.rationale: It identifies customer relationships, workflow integration, and learning from real usage as sources of durable advantage, contrasting them with access to a model everyone can use.

sol-6.1.text:
I would first separate two questions: where will AGI create value, and who will actually capture that value? Those might have very different answers. A technology can be enormously useful while competition makes it difficult for investors to earn attractive returns.

If I were allocating $50 billion, I wouldn’t feel obligated to invest all of it immediately. I’d look across compute, models, and applications, and ask where there is a durable advantage. For infrastructure, that means understanding demand, depreciation, and how quickly today’s hardware could become obsolete. For model companies, it means asking whether better capabilities translate into a sustainable business, given how quickly competitors can catch up.

Personally, I’d be particularly interested in applications where intelligence can complete valuable work. But a compelling demo isn’t enough. Can the system reliably finish a task? Can you measure the economic value? Does the company have access to customers and a workflow that improves as the technology improves?

So I’d invest in stages, preserve substantial capital, and increase commitments as those questions become clearer. With $50 billion, the advantage is that you can afford to be patient. You don’t have to predict one winner today.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare companies holding user context to oil companies before cars were invented.

r002.rationale: It discusses durable advantages generally, but does not say that owning user context creates a moat if AI intelligence becomes broadly accessible.
